title: CLAY COUNTY PROPERTY TAXES
full_story:
The first installment of the 2025 taxes payable in 2026 is due Friday, October 16th.  The second installment is due on Friday, November 20th.

Payment can be made to the Clay County Treasurer using any of the following options, by mail, send your check with the payment stub to the Clay County Treasurer PO Box 88 Louisville, IL 62858.  Mailed payments must be postmarked on or before the due date to avoid penalty.  You can pay at the treasurer’s office in the Clay County Courthouse where they accept cash, checks, cashier’s checks, or money orders.  Please bring your entire bill if you want it stamped to show proof of payment.  Office hours are 8:00 am – 4:00 pm Monday through Friday.  Online payments can be made by credit/debit card by going to govpaynow.com PLC #a00082, there will be a convenience fee charged for online Credit Card payments.  Payment can also be made by placing your payment in the envelope depository at the north entrance of the Clay County Courthouse.  Please include payment stub.

For questions call Clay County Treasurer Stacey Allen’s office at 618-665-3727.

title: SHADOWS OF ELMWOOD
full_story:
Flora Rotary will be hosting its 12th annual Shadows of Elmwood Cemetery Tour this Friday and Saturday.  Tickets will be available at the Flora Depot.

Ticket sales will start just before 5 pm with the first wagon leaving at 5 each night.  Tickets are sold until 9 pm and the wagons will go until the last patron has gone through.  Tickets are $8 each unless you purchase a Benefactor Ticket at $25 and go to the front of the line to get on the next available wagon.

The club will also have ride assist tickets for those unable to ride on the hay wagons.  If you are physically unable to ride the wagon, they will have spots available on golf carts that will follow the wagons through the cemetery.  Tickets are reserved for those who are in need, and available on a first come first served basis.

While you wait at the Depot there will be 2 additional skits to keep you entertained and there will be concessions available from Krazy Sweet Treats and Kernel Pops.

All proceeds from the cemetery tour go to Flora Rotary for their projects in the community.  The Rotary Club is currently working on updating Flora Rotary Park and adding improvements at Flora’s Pickleball Courts.

full_story:

title: EFFINGHAM MAN CHARGED
full_story:
Attorney General Kwame Raoul charged an Effingham, Illinois man with possessing child sexual abuse material.  The case is part of Raoul’s ongoing work, in collaboration with federal law enforcement agencies and local law enforcement officials throughout Illinois, to apprehend offenders who download and trade child sexual abuse material online.

The Attorney General’s office charged Travis J. Gillespie, 54, in Effingham County Circuit Court with two Class 1 counts of possession of child sexual abuse material, each punishable by up to 15 years in prison.  Gillespie is detained at the Effingham County Jail, and his next court date is September 17th.

Raoul’s investigators, along with officers from the Effingham Police Department and the Illinois Law Enforcement Alarm System (ILEAS), conducted a search on Thursday of Gillespie’s residence in Effingham.  Gillespie was arrested after evidence of child sexual abuse material was found.

“Crimes involving the exploitation of children are among the most serious offenses law enforcement is called upon to investigate.  The Effingham Police Department is grateful for the diligent work and expertise of the Illinois Attorney General’s Office and for the opportunity to assist with this investigation,” said Effingham Police Chief Kurt Davis.

Raoul’s office is prosecuting the case with Effingham County State’s Attorney Aaron Jones’s office.

The public is reminded that the defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.

title: WAYNE COUNTY NLID PROJECT
full_story:
When Wayne County farmer Fred Blessing received a call from his county Farm Bureau manager about hosting a new research project, he didn’t hesitate to say yes.

“I said, ‘Yeah, I’d be glad to be a part of it,’” Blessing told FarmWeek of how the Nutrient Loss Inhibitor Demonstration (NLID) research project got its start on his corn and soybean farm about 10 years ago.

The NLID plot, a partnership with the Wayne County Farm Bureau, Wabash Valley Service Co. and Illinois Farm Bureau, helps researchers evaluate nutrient enhancers, inhibitors and micro and secondary nutrients.  The goal is to help farmers improve fertilizer efficiency and determine which practices provide the greatest economic return.

Blessing said research findings led him to adopt cover crops to “grab a hold” of excess nitrogen left in the soil following a lower-yield year.  But one of the project’s biggest takeaways so far has been sulfur trials that showed a positive yield response in corn.

“Since then, every acre of our corn gets sulfur on it,” he said.

The NLID project on the Blessing farm is a part of a statewide effort to track corn’s response to nitrogen to refine Maximum Return to Nitrogen (MRTN) recommendations for farmers.  John Pike, a research agronomist and certified crop adviser with Pike Ag LLC, works with the Illinois Fertilizer and Chemical Association and John Jones from the Crop Sciences Department at the University of Illinois to coordinate these trials; funded through the Nutrient Research Education Council; on about 10 to 15 sites across southern Illinois.

“While the results of the research trials are of interest to the specific farms that cooperate in the project, having a number of these sites across a particular region and the state as a whole allows nitrogen response to be observed according to the variety of soils, planting date and weather variables that impact crop yields in a given season,” he said.

Pike added that the Blessing plot, which he joined about eight years ago, continues to serve as the host site for the county’s NLID Field Day.  He said the annual event helps keep farmers updated on “what’s coming from Fred’s farm” and how data collected there contributes to research across the region.

This year’s field day, held on August 20th, was a part of IFB’s series of summer Nutrient Loss Reduction Strategy Field Days held across Illinois.

In addition to presentations from Blessing and Pike, other guest speakers included CEO of BAM Weather Michael Clark, who spoke on making high-cost decisions based on forecasts generated by his team, and IFB Director of Environmental Policy Sanjay Sofat, who discussed Minnesota’s response to nitrate contamination in drinking water and the steps Illinois farmers can take to stay ahead of similar water quality changes.

Mike Wilson from the Wabash Valley Service Co. addressed the unique set of challenges 2026 brought, including weather-related challenges and the war in Iran, which disrupted shipments of oil, fertilizer and natural gas.  But despite these challenges, operations on Blessing’s NLID plot “couldn’t have gone better.”

“Each year we strive to provide real-world, on-farm data that our farmers can use when making decisions for their own operations.  We have seen many of our farmers adjust their fertilizer strategies based on the information they learned from our NLID project,” said Doug Anderson, manager of the Wayne County Farm Bureau, and a speaker at this year’s event.  “We are grateful to the Illinois Farm Bureau for continuing to support our NLID project, now in its 10th year.  The work we are doing is important to our members.”

After the final harvest data is collected, the post-harvest summary of the 2026 NLID plot will be available at waynecfb.com/nlid.

title: COMMUNITY CHOIR REHEARSALS
full_story:
For 16 seasons, the Olney Central College Community Choir has brought together singers from across Southeastern Illinois to share their voices, build friendships and experience the joy of making music together.

OCC Director of Choral Activities Dr. Andrew Pittman invites new and returning singers to become part of the tradition when rehearsals begin at 6 pm on September 8th.

“There is something special about making music together,” he said.  “To share the joy of singing together and to experience that visceral sense of connection that happens when voices come together is truly unique.”

The choir offers an opportunity for fellowship and camaraderie while giving singers the chance to learn, grow and perform alongside others who share a love of music.  High school-age singers and older are welcome to participate, and no audition is required.  The only requirements are the ability to carry a tune and, most importantly, a desire to sing.

“I think one of the most rewarding things about the Community Choir is seeing people come in at the beginning of the semester and watching their confidence grow,” Pittman added.

Rehearsals will be held from 6 to 8 pm on Tuesdays in Room 216, the OCC Choir/Band Room, on the second floor of Dr. Kent L. Wattleworth Hall.  The choir will present its annual Christmas Concert at 7 pm on December 3rd in the Dr. John D. Stull Performing Arts Center.

To register for the OCC Community Choir, call 618-395-7777 as soon as possible.

title: GRAZING SCHOOLS
full_story:
The Illinois Grazing Lands Coalition (ILGLC) will host two grazing schools in September to give farmers around the state hands-on, practical instruction to help them implement and expand managed grazing on their operations.

The events will be held at the Evan Schuette beef cattle farm in Iuka on Saturday and Greg Thoren’s beef cattle farm in Stockton on Friday, September 18th.

Each school combines classroom-style instruction with in-field, pasture-based learning led by the host farmers, ILGLC staff and other experienced graziers.  Topics will focus on soil and pasture health, basics of adaptive grazing, water and fencing systems, multispecies grazing and winter grazing strategies.

Registration is $25 per attendee and is required in advance.  Visit the website ilgrazinglands.org/events to register or for more information.

title: TREE STAND PERMITS AVAILABLE
full_story:
Lake Shelbyville’s tree stand policy for this year will remain the same as last season’s policy.

The policy allows hunters to leave one stand up for the season, referred to as a seasonal tree stand, and/or use up to two roving stands that may be left up during archery season for no more than 72 hours without use, or the length of a three-day weekend.  Seasonal tree stands may be placed two weeks before archery season and must be removed within two weeks after archery season ends.  Archery season runs from October 1st, through January 17th.

Hunters wishing to purchase a seasonal tree stand permit must present a valid hunting license before a permit is issued.  Seasonal tree stand permits will be available for purchase for $30 by credit or debit card at the Lake Shelbyville Project Office, 1989 State Hwy. 16, Shelbyville, Illinois, from 8 am to 4:30 pm Monday through Friday.

Roving tree stand permits are free and may be obtained in Sullivan, Illinois, at Ace Hardware, Chip’s Marine, or Sullivan 66, formerly Howy’s Lakeside, located five miles south of Sullivan on Highway 32.  Hunters may also pick up roving tree stand permits at the Lake Shelbyville Project Office, Ace Hardware and Craig’s Sporting Goods in Shelbyville.

For more information about the Lake Shelbyville tree stand policy, contact the Environmental Stewardship Department at 217-774-3951, ext. 7049.
